analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off California, Oregon, and Washington.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently bar new offshore drilling off the West Coast never got a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from ever issuing a new lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in federal waters off the coasts of California, Oregon, and Washington [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by Sen. Dianne Feinstein with nine cosponsors on January 27, 2021, and was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it [S1] [S5]. It expired when that Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing businesses, tourism-dependent communities, and the general public along the West Coast, who would be protected from the oil-spill and pollution risks that come with offshore drilling. The bill would also lock in a permanent legal barrier rather than leaving West Coast waters exposed to whichever future administration opens a new leasing plan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: West Coast coastal communities and ocean economies

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a subsection to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act directing that the Secretary of the Interior 'shall not issue a lease for the exploration, development, or production of oil or natural gas' in any federal waters off California, Oregon, or Washington [S3].

Because the ban is written into statute and overrides any other provision of law, it would permanently close those waters to new drilling rather than leaving the decision to each administration's five-year leasing plans [S2] [S3].

Keeping new drilling out of West Coast waters protects the fisheries, beaches, and tourism that coastal economies depend on from the risk of oil spills and drilling infrastructure, the way a ban on drilling protects the resource those businesses live off.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would be permanently shut out of new leasing in West Coast federal waters, and the federal treasury, which forgoes potential bonus bids, rents, and royalties from any future leases there. Broader energy consumers bear a negligible cost, since these waters are a tiny share of U.S. production potential.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently removes a domestic energy source from development, forgoing potential federal royalties and any future production, which is the core objection raised whenever West Coast drilling bans come up [S3].
The ban reaches only new leases: it does not cancel drilling under existing federal leases off California, so current operations could continue [S2].

A permanent statutory ban forecloses revisiting the question even if future conditions — technology, safety records, or energy markets — change materially, which critics of drilling moratoriums argue is too rigid for a statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — permanent legal protection for West Coast waters, beaches, and fisheries from new drilling and spill risk — is broad and durable, and the cost is limited to forgone potential drilling revenue in an area that is not a major production frontier. The main honest criticism is rigidity: a statute can never be revisited, and the bill leaves existing leases untouched. On balance the trade is small local and industry costs for a large, permanent public benefit — but none of it happened, because the bill died in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never scheduled action on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on January 27, 2021, with nine cosponsors — eight Senate Democrats and one independent — and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.

The committee took no further action: the bill's entire action history is introduction and referral, with no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote through the end of the 117th Congress.
Because no version of the bill passed the Senate, the House never considered it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests kept West Coast federal waters open as a possible future leasing area, since no permanent statutory ban was enacted; coastal communities got no new legal protection beyond the policies already in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drilling interests kept future access open

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the West Coast Ocean Protection Act and promoted it at introduction.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, including Sens. Padilla, Wyden, Merkley, Murray, Cantwell, Menendez, Booker, Markey, and Sanders.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Joe Manchin (D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it dead in committee for the full two years of the Congress.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Industry whose West Coast leasing prospects the bill would eliminate
against.what_they_did: No lobbying campaign on this specific bill appears in the record; the industry broadly opposes statutory drilling bans on the Outer Continental Shelf.

sides.party_line_note: All ten original sponsors were Democrats or independents, and no Republican cosponsored; with no vote ever taken, the partisan split is visible only in sponsorship, not in a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar these companies from obtaining any new lease to explore for or produce oil and gas in federal waters off California, Oregon, and Washington [S3]. Their interest in opening those waters to drilling runs against the coastal public's interest in keeping its beaches and fisheries spill-free.

industries.industry: West Coast fishing and seafood businesses
industries.note: A statutory ban on new drilling lowers the risk of oil spills and drilling activity in the waters where these businesses fish; their fortunes rise and fall with the health of the same ocean the public uses.

industries.industry: West Coast tourism and coastal recreation economies
industries.note: Beaches and coastal tourism depend on unpolluted waters; permanently closing the area to new leasing protects that asset, the same interest ordinary coastal residents hold.
